summary: Describes extensions to OSPF so routers can forward IP multicast datagrams, building delivery trees from the link-state database OSPF already maintains. It was written as a standards-track proposal. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a mail carrier who knows the whole town map. This lets the carrier copy one letter and send it down just the streets where people asked to get it.

questions: how does multicast work in ospf
how does multicast routing work in ospf
what is a wild-card multicast receiver
subtitle: How OSPF routers can forward IP multicast by building a pruned shortest-path tree for each source and group.

tldr.problem: OSPF routes unicast traffic only, so it could not carry IP multicast datagrams to every member of a group spread over many networks.
tldr.mechanism: A new link state advertisement, the group-membership-LSA, records where group members are. Each router then builds, on demand, a shortest-path tree rooted at the datagram's source, prunes branches with no members, and caches the result.
tldr.outcome: The memo was a standards-track proposal and is now Historic. Multicast support could be added to an OSPF domain piecemeal, but non-multicast routers could cause suboptimal paths or lost delivery.

today: RFC 1584 is marked Historic. It was published as a standards-track proposal in March 1994, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It builds on RFC 1583 (OSPF Version 2).

sections.title: Multicast on Top of OSPF
sections.content:
RFC 1584 defines MOSPF, a set of backward-compatible additions to OSPF Version 2 for routing IP multicast. Multicast groups are class D addresses and hosts join them with IGMP, as set out in RFC 1112. MOSPF carries a multicast datagram from one network to another through routers.

MOSPF routes on both the datagram's source and destination. The OSPF link state database already describes the whole topology of the Autonomous System. Adding one new advertisement, the group-membership-LSA, pins down where group members are, so a router can compute the datagram's path.

Routers with the extensions interoperate with plain OSPF routers for unicast traffic. There is no way to tunnel multicast through non-multicast routers, and datagrams are forwarded as is, never encapsulated.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF already gives every router a map of the network. MOSPF adds notes on the map saying which places want which group's messages, so routers can send copies only where they are wanted.

sections.title: Forwarding with Shortest-Path Trees
sections.content:
A datagram follows the least-cost path from its source to each group member, with cost taken from the OSPF metric. Where member paths share a segment the datagram travels once, and it is copied only where the paths diverge. All routers calculate an identical tree, so there is no equal-cost multipath.

Each router decides using a forwarding cache with one entry per source and destination pair. An entry names the upstream node the datagram must arrive from and the downstream interfaces to send it out of. The entry is built from two parts: the local group database (members on directly attached networks, learned through IGMP) and the datagram's pruned shortest-path tree.

Only the Designated Router on a network sends IGMP Host Membership Queries and listens to Reports, so a network appears in at most one router's local group database and datagrams are not delivered twice. Each router then floods a group-membership-LSA for each group that has local members.

The tree is built when the first datagram arrives, rooted at the source's network, and branches holding no labelled router or transit network are pruned. Each downstream interface carries a hop count so that an expanding ring search, where a host raises the IP TTL step by step, does not waste bandwidth. The whole cache is cleared when the topology changes, and a group's entries are cleared when its membership LSAs change.

On non-broadcast networks, where there is no data-link multicast, the datagram is sent separately to each downstream neighbor. IGMP is not defined there, so no group members can sit directly on such a network.
sections.plainLanguage: When the first letter for a club arrives, the carrier draws the shortest routes to every club member, crosses out streets with no members, and keeps the drawing for next time.

sections.title: Areas and Other Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
Group-membership-LSAs are flooded within a single OSPF area only. A subset of area border routers, the inter-area multicast forwarders, summarize each non-backbone area's group membership into the backbone. This is asymmetric: the information is not re-advertised into other non-backbone areas, and the backbone's membership is not summarized for them.

To make up for that, inter-area multicast forwarders are wild-card multicast receivers in non-backbone areas. They receive all multicast traffic whatever its destination, so every datagram from a non-backbone area reaches the backbone, which knows all the groups.

Because a router sees only part of the topology, the neighborhood of a source in another area is approximated with OSPF summary links, and a source in another Autonomous System with multicast-capable AS external links. In those cases the links in the tree point back toward the source, which assumes the inter-AS multicast protocol forwards in a reverse path forwarding fashion. The RFC notes this can give suboptimal routing with asymmetric costs and can even cause non-delivery with asymmetric reachability.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighborhood keeps its own list of who wants what, and one helper per neighborhood takes every letter to the central post office, where the full list lives.

sections.title: The Group-Membership-LSA and Option Bits
sections.content:
The group-membership-LSA is the Type 6 link state advertisement. It uses the standard 20-byte LSA header, with the Link State ID set to the destination multicast group. It is followed by a list of transit vertices to label, each a Vertex type (1 for a router, 2 for a transit network) and a Vertex ID. There is no metric.

For a router vertex the ID is its OSPF Router ID, and the only router that may be listed is the advertising router. For a transit network it is the IP address of the network's Designated Router.

Two bits carry multicast information. The new MC bit in the OSPF Options field marks multicast capability: only advertisements with it set are used to calculate multicast paths, and it tells neighbors in Database Description packets whether the router takes part in flooding group-membership-LSAs. The new W bit in the router-LSA's rtype field marks a wild-card multicast receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note on the map says which group it is for and which stops on the map have members. Two little flags tell others whether a router speaks multicast and whether it wants every letter.

sections.title: Mixed Networks and Configuration
sections.content:
MOSPF routers can be mixed with plain OSPF routers, which allows gradual deployment. Non-multicast routers are left out of the trees and do not flood group-membership-LSAs. The RFC warns that unicast connectivity may then exist without multicast connectivity, that a non-multicast Designated Router stops a network carrying multicast, and that multicast and unicast paths can diverge, making problems harder to debug. It recommends keeping every router in an area with the same multicast and TOS capabilities.

The per-interface IPMulticastForwarding parameter can be disabled, data-link multicast (the default) or data-link unicast. The non-default values handle several IP subnets on one wire and networks on Autonomous System boundaries, where two multicast protocols could deliver duplicates. MOSPF can also build a separate tree per IP Type of Service, falling back to the TOS 0 tree if the TOS 0 tree contains a TOS-incapable router.

An implementation needs promiscuous multicast reception, a way to tell data-link multicast from unicast, and IGMP.
sections.plainLanguage: New and old routers can work in the same town. Old ones just get skipped when copies of letters are sent, so it works best if everyone in a neighborhood has the same skills.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It adds no authentication or protection of its own for the group-membership-LSAs it introduces.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not say anything about keeping this safe from tricksters.
